Arduino platform is based on a range of microcontroller interface boards especially designed for those new to microcontrollers or those who would not normally build electronic circuits, and those that need to do quick prototyping. The truth is that an Arduino can be used by almost anyone and in addition to its obvious uses it can serve as a learning tool, and the large amount of software available for the various Arduino boards takes away a lot of the difficulty in getting started with something new. Whatever your needs, someone else may have already tackled a similar project and you can use their work (with permission/crediting as necessary) which gives you a head start but of course you can also try yourself from scratch, which is a good way to get to grips with new hardware. </span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The Arduino home page can be found at:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://www.arduino.cc/" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://www.arduino.cc/</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Arduinos are good for prototyping rather than for projects that are supposed to endure long use although they have been used successfully in semi-permanent installations. Once you have got what you set out to do working with an Arduino you can then design (or have someone else do the design) a more permanent version if that's your intention rather than just trying something out.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Another use for an Arduino is for testing components (an LCD, for example) as likely the code for using the component has already been made, so you can just download the code, connect up what you are testing and you'll quickly know whether it's working or is suitable for what you want to make.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Please see YouTuber </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-style: italic;">I Like To Make Stuff</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Overview</span></div></h2><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">There are a number of different official Arduino boards including the Uno, Mega and Nano, which you can check out on the official page:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://www.arduino.cc/en/hardware" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="font-variant: normal; text-decoration: underline;">https://www.arduino.cc/en/hardware</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">There are also</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;"> clones that are directly based on the official boards, as Arduino is open source so anyone can make their own version of an Arduino and sell it but it is always encouraged to buy an official Arduino board to support the original designers </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">and the clones may have subtle differences (for example, one clone I have runs at a slower speed than the official board). </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">You can also find Arduino boards tailored to a certain need (such as for robot projects or 3D printer)</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">, as well as boards that have some form of compatibility with Arduino but are otherwise very different in architecture -</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;"> please see the Compatible boards section of this page.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Each of the Arduino boards has different features, such as the amount of memory, the speed of the microcontroller, the size of the board and the number and type of I/O connections (for connecting lights, switches, etc.). The Arduino Uno is usually the first Arduino a beginner uses but for more complicated projects the Arduino Mega is better as it offers more I/O connections. The Arduino Nano is similar to the Uno but is </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">s</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">maller and unlike the Uno the Nano fits into standard size breadboard thanks to the male header pins. Then there are more advanced boards, including the </span><a class="XqQF9c" href="/site/jamesskingdom/Home/electronics-by-james-s/interfacing/arduino-yún" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="font-variant: normal; text-decoration: underline;">Arduino Yún</span></a><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">, which are ideal for Internet of Things (IoT) applications due to its built-in support for networking and powerful processor combined with a traditional microcontroller.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">The programming language used with the Arduino is called Wiring and is similar to C/C++ with gives access to reading from and writing to the </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I/O</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;"> pins as well as for configuration</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">, and the programs you write or obtain from other people are called 'sketches'.</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;"> After a sketch (program) is written on a computer, it can be uploaded to an attached Arduino and then the program will run automatically after the board resets (or at least that is the behaviour for mo</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">st</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;"> Arduino boards). Since an Arduino board typically can be programmed 100,000 times you can make changes as often as needed. Like with most microcontrollers, the program code for the Arduino is stored in flash memory (like what is used in SD cards) on board the microcontroller on the Arduino board; you get 32KB on the standard Arduino Uno, for e</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">xample</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Going into more detail about the Arduino Uno as it's a good starting point,</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""> you can check out its official page at:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://store.arduino.cc/products/arduino-uno-rev3" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://store.arduino.cc/products/arduino-uno-rev3</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">As you can see it uses an 8-bit ATmega328P microcontroller running at 16MHz, has 14 digital I/O pins (of which 6 support PWM), 6 analog inputs, 32KB flash memory, 2KB SRAM,  1KB EEPROM, and an on-board LED connected to digital pin 13, useful for debugging. The board measures 68.6 x 53.4 mm, weighs 25g, and</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;"> it has two rows of connectors which provide power, and interface in the form of digital I/O lines that can be programmed as either inputs or outputs, and a number of analogue inputs. You can plug wires into theses sockets, although it's best to use the type with pins either end so that the wires stay in place. You can also plug in a circuit board known as a shield which has a number of headers for connecting with the Arduino. You can buy these shields ready made designed for a set task (for example wireless communications) or there are ones available with a matrix of holes for soldering your own components. You could make up a shield yourself using stripboard although I found that some connections didn't quite line up so I had to bend the header pins somewhat. If you do buy a shield then make sure it's compatible with your Arduino.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Whereas most of the Arduino boards use an 8-bit Atmel microcontroller, the Arduino Due (for example) breaks with that tradition as it uses a 32-bit ARM microcontroller. It has an impressive spec but its logic level is at 3.3V (as opposed to the 5V logic level of the 8-bit Arduinos). This means that interfacing with non 3.3V devices-including non Due Arduinos-can harm an Arduino Due. The workaround is by using a logic level shifting circuit to make sure the Arduino Due is interfaced only with 3.3V logic.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">While the Arduino is great for taking away some of the difficulty of interfacing microcontrollers with input and output devices, you pay a price for that convenience; I'll explain why. Microcontrollers, like other processors run on machine language, which are the binary values (0's and 1's) that make up the low-level instructions that form the microcontroller's program. You can program a microcontroller in assembly language, which consists of a number of instructions that represent the machine language values, and are more readable than a bunch of 0's and 1's, or even the hexadecimal equivalents (i.e. 5F, CE, etc.). Assembly language gives you great control over the microcontroller as well as optimum speed but assembly language is more difficult to use and not recommended for beginners.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">So, the Arduino team went with a more high level programming language (Wiring) that is more easier to use than assembly language but the Wiring code gets converted into machine language before being uploaded to the Arduino. It's this converting that can cause programs written for the Arduino to run slower than if the chip had been programmed directly in assembly language. The conversion process is optimised, that is, the assembly language instructions are chosen to give as high speed as possible. What introduces slow down is that some Wiring commands, such as the digitalWrite() function, have to do error checking, which means more assembly language instructions are required, slowing down how fast the program runs.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Fortunately, the Wiring programming language provides a way to more directly access the Arduino ports, giving greater speed at the expense of getting closer to the hardware level of the Arduino which may be confusing to those new to the Arduino or microcontrollers in general. </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I'll link to a page that gives details but it's something you may want to come back to when you've have a greater understanding of typical Arduino architecture:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://docs.arduino.cc/retired/hacking/software/PortManipulation/" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://docs.arduino.cc/retired/hacking/software/PortManipulation/</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">f you are doing something simple such as flashing an LED, digitalWrite() and similar functions will give you all the speed you need. But if you need greater speed, such as to update a large display frequently, if may be that you will have to use a more low-level means of accessing the Arduino's ports. If you do use the low level commands your program will likely take up less space than if you had used the high level functions.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">In summary. t</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">he process of building an Arduino circuit is writing the Wiring code (or downloading) using a PC and then transferring the code to the Arduino (usually using USB). Lights, switches, and so on can then be connected to the Arduino to complete the circuit but do so </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-style: italic; font-variant: normal;">after</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;"> removing power to the Arduino. Also, before powering up the Arduino again, check and double check you have wired it up correctly. It's </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">a good idea to use</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;"> coloured wires to help prevent mistakes such as red for positive power supply line, black for a ground connection, for example.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I recommend that you view YouTuber SunFounder Maker Education's video and the follow up ones from the same channel to help cement the basics of using an Arduino:</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section 22R)</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">x1 ATtint85 in chip holder</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Note that older versions of the board used mini USB instead of full size USB-B, and the kit used to come with two clear body LEDs, which perhaps caused some confusion (not that it's hard to test them to determine the colour) whereas my kit came with a single clear body LED which lights up red, as well as a green body LED.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Since the board is very small and the various components are packed together it's perhaps not the best soldering kit for beginners but if you have experience like me you shouldn't have trouble. This was the order I soldered the components; resistors, ceramic capacitor, diodes, LEDs (green for power, red for stat), reset switch, electrolytic cap, IC socket, header, USB socket. It took me 45 minutes to solder the kit, carefully following the instructions online, note that the online manual still mentions a USB mini connector on page 8, which was used in the original design.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">After finishing the soldering and before putting the microcontroller chip in the socket I plugged the board into a USB power adapter and made sure the power LED came on. I also measured the voltage between pin 8 (VCC) and 4 (GND) of the IC socket, which was 3.8V. This is correct, as there's 2 diodes in series with VCC and USB +5V, which brings the microcontroller voltage down low enough such that its I/O will operate at 3.3V, in line with USB spec, although there is no USB controller, instead the microcontroller emulates USB using V-USB.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Even with everything soldered and checked I quickly found it difficult to program the board, which unfortunately is my second experience of having trouble getting an Olimex product to work, the first being an FPGA board (but I was successful eventually). Looking online a lot of people have had trouble getting the kit to work but whether it was the same fault as me - which you can read about toward the end of this section, which led me to successfully programming the board - isn't clear. One potential problem with the OLIMEXINO-85-KIT is that it appears to originally be from 2014 and because it uses V-USB, it doesn't play nicely with modern operating systems (or Windows, at least), but again, not the issue for me once I fixed the fault.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The OLIMEXINO-85-KIT is supposedly preloaded with the "micronucleus tiny85" bootloader, which is similar to a typical Arduino bootloader but designed especially for the AVR ATtiny microcontroller family, and is meant to make it easy to upload sketches to the microcontroller using the Arduino IDE. You can find the GitHub page at:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://github.com/micronucleus/micronucleus" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://github.com/micronucleus/micronucleus</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Looking at the user manual for programming the board it says that we need to use a modified version of the Arduino IDE to upload code to it but because the bootloader is also used by the Digispark board we can use the same instructions. This is the link that is provided in the manual that explains how to install the drivers and set up the Arduino IDE to be able to program the board:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="http://digistump.com/wiki/digispark/tutorials/connecting" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">http://digistump.com/wiki/digispark/tutorials/connecting</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Rather than a 'modified' version of the IDE, you download and install the normal Arduino IDE (if you don't already have it), and then you download and install the digistump driver. Then, in the Arduino IDE you add the Digistump AVR Boards using the Boards manager and during the installation the Device Driver Installation Wizard will pop up but for me (I'm using Windows 10) it showed an error: 'Digistump LLC (usbser) Ports' install failed. The same error can be seen here:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://arduino.stackexchange.com/questions/30003/digispark-usb-issue" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://arduino.stackexchange.com/questions/30003/digispark-usb-issue</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I did come across this page:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://github.com/ArminJo/DigistumpArduino" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://github.com/ArminJo/DigistumpArduino</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Which has a different boards manager URL allowing access to V1.7.6:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArminJo/DigistumpArduino/master/package_digistump_index.json" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ArminJo/DigistumpArduino/master/package_digistump_index.json</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">That was also unsuccessful but from what other people have said online it doesn't matter if one of the drivers (the top one in the </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Device Driver Installation Wizard</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">) doesn't successfully install as it's a duplicate anyway. So I modified the built-in Blink example by changing LED_BUILTIN to 1, as that's what the board's stat LED's connected to, and if the driver isn't the issue I should still be able to program the board but it's not like an ordinary Arduino which you plug into your computer's USB and then click 'Upload' in the Arduino IDE. With the OLIMEXINO-85-KIT you have to first have the board disconnected from your computer's USB, click 'Upload' in the Arduino IDE and you will be prompted to plug in the board within the given time, and then the board will be programmed. However, for me (and a lot of other people) that never happens, the board is never detected it times out and Windows pops up with 'Unknown USB Device (Device Descriptor Request Failed)' error. The stat LED will flash a few times on the board, which is supposedly a sign the bootloader is running, but the Arduino IDE will not detect the board.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I've tried multiple Windows 10 computers and even a Windows 8 computer, and current and older versions of the Arduino IDE (as far back as V1.6.5., which is recommended in the</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;"> OLIMEXINO-85-KIT </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">manual, and the most recent at the time, V2.1.1), </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">without success</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""> but unfortunately I don't have a Windows 7 computer as I wondered if the bootloader is so old it doesn't like anything newer than Windows 7. Someone online did suggest plugging the board into a hub with the reasoning being that it's a problem with USB 3 and the hub will effectively downgrade to USB 2 (so, has to be a USB 2 hub) but that didn't help me.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Another step I tried also without success: setting the programmer to micronucleus in the Arduino IDE but that made no difference and supposedly is an unnecessary step.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Before arriving at the ultimate solution I did look online and found a site which details how to program the microcontroller directly using an Arduino as an ISP (In-System Programmer) programmer along with </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">the Attiny </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">p</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">ackage</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="http://dumbpcs.blogspot.com/2015/11/programming-your-attiny85-with-arduino.html" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">http://dumbpcs.blogspot.com/2015/11/programming-your-attiny85-with-arduino.html</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">header pins as follows:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Arduino</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><span style="">#2</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Don't forget the 10uF capacitor on the Arduino reset and GND pins. Because the connection between the OLIMEXINO-85-KIT reset header pin is open (on my version of the board, at least) you need to solder a bridge across RST_E on the underside of the board so it may be easier to put the microcontroller into breadboard and wire it up as shown on the site previously linked, which is what I did.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Before uploading the blink sketch as a test I changed LED_BUILTIN to 1 to be compatible with the </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">OLIMEXINO-85-KIT</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">'s on-board user LED.  As I was using Arduino IDE V2.1.1 I had to select Sketch->Upload Using Programmer (otherwise you get 'a programmer is required to upload' error'. This actually starts the upload process (if using the new IDE) and the IDE then reported it had written to flash, which only took a few seconds. When I put the chip back in the </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">OLIMEXINO-85-KIT board </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">and connected it to my PCB the LED flashed briefly as before, </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">as if the original bootloader is still running,</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""> but when I put the chip into breadboard and connected an LED and resistor to pin 6 (output 1) with the Arduino powering the chip (all other I/O pins still connected to the </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Arduino </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">) the LED flashes rapidly unless pin 1 (reset) is taken to GND. This is odd as the LED should flash on/off every second but otherwise the code upload appears to have worked.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">It seems the issue is that the internal clock needs to be set to 8MHz, which involves using the Burn bootloader option (although it doesnt actually burn a bootloader but instead sets various options in the chip). This isn't explained on the dumbpcs site but is in the page it links to:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="http://highlowtech.org/?p=1695" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">http://highlowtech.org/?p=1695</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Under 'Configuring the ATtiny to run at 8 MHz'.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Then upload the sketch and the LED will flash on/off every second. I further tested by changing the Blink sketch so that the LED turns on/off every 5 seconds (change the delay value from 1000 to 5000). I then selected the 'Upload Using Programmer' option again and it compiled and uploaded and when I reconnected the LED to pin 6 it flashed on/off </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">every </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">5 seconds. Oddly, if I put the chip back in the </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">OLIMEXINO-85-KIT</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">, whether I connect the board's USB to my PC or a power supply, the stat LED doesn't flash as I programmed it to but the LED does blink a few times when you connect the OLIMEXINO to a PC.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Back to the original problem: after first soldering the kit I had measured the power supply pins of the microcontroller and since I had got an acceptable reading it had seemed there wasn't a fault with my soldering but it shows how important it is to visually </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">check your soldering very carefully </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">as well as by other means as when I checked the supply pins again the reading was too low. It turns out there was a bad solder joint on pin 4 (GND) of the IC socket, which must have been passable initially. The bad solder joint turned out to be the reason why I couldn't program the board when it had the bootloader installed and the reason that the stat LED didn't flash even after programming the microcontroller directly using an </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Arduino</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""> while the microcontroller was in breadboard.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Now that the solder joint was fixed, measuring again across the IC power supply pins once more I got 3.62V (this was with the chip installed in the socket) and the LED was flashing off/on as I had programmed it to via the Arduino as an ISP programmer. I also checked and indeed the board now worked whether powered over USB or through the header pins. With the board fixed I should have been able to program it over USB but as I had programmed the microcontroller directly the bootloader was wiped, one sign of which is that the when the board is powered the stat LED turns on immediately without any delay unlike if there was a bootloader present. So the next step was to put the bootloader back on, the process is explained on page 10 of the user manual and it involves downloading the required files from the </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">OLIMEXINO-85-KIT</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""> main page, the link is called 'OLIMEXINO-85 demo examples, libraries and bootloader binaries are available at our GitHub repository'. The link is takes you to is:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://github.com/OLIMEX/OLIMEXINO-85/tree/master/SOFTWARE" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://github.com/OLIMEX/OLIMEXINO-85/tree/master/SOFTWARE</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">There are both hex and elf files, the elf file is better as it contains the required fuse and configuration bits, which determine various settings on the microcontroller, and if set wrong, can cause major issues with using the microcontroller but fortunately the OLIMEXINO-85-KIT gives the required fuse settings. The Micronucleus bootloader that is recommended to use is V1.06 from 8 years ago, the manual warns against using a newer version.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The manual, however, doesn't detail the hardware setup to program the bootloader but I was successful using the TL866CS MiniPro programmer, here are the steps I used:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Open the MiniPro software (I used v6.85), select ATTINY85 as Device, click on the Config tab and make these changes:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Check 'SELFPRGEN=0' under 'Extended Fuse Byte', you should see 'Extended Fuse Byte' value at the bottom of the window change to 0xFE under IC Config Information.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Check 'BODLEVEL1=0' under 'Fuse High Byte', 'Fuse High Byte' value will become 0xDD.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Uncheck 'CKSEL0' and check 'CKSEL1' under 'Fuse Low Byte', 'Fuse Low Byte' value will become 0xE1.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">For reference, here are the fuse settings in visual style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Load the hex file previously downloaded from the previously linked </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">GitH</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">ub page, in the 'File load Options' pop-up window select 'INTEL HEX' for File Format. Then Program the chip. In the 'Chip Program' pop-up window uncheck 'LOCK Bit' (not necessary but best to be safe you don't accidentally change the lock bits). The programming should happen very quickly.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">After following those steps I put the microcontroller back into the board and connected it to my PC's USB, the stat LED was off and then after 5 seconds it flashed on/off about every second, perhaps a built-in test program. I then modified the Arduino Blink sketch to flash every 5 seconds, clicked upload, connected the board and after a couple of seconds it started uploading and finished after a few seconds. The stat LED then started blinking every 5 seconds as expected, showing a successful sketch upload.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Note that the output of the Arduino window says it detected firmware version 1.6 but I'm not sure if that's actually V1.06, as I can't find V1.6 online.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Even though I had problems initially programming the OLIMEXINO-85-KIT due to a bad solder joint I did get it working as we've seen and to add, on a Windows 10 Surface Pro using its USB 3 port, so it is very much possible to use the kit with more modern computers.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Now that I was able to upload sketches to the OLIMEXINO-85-KIT using the Arduino IDE I went on to further test the microcontroller and see if I could get the remaining I/O pins working. I modified the Blink sketch and set I/O numbers 0 to 2 as outputs (the numbered I/O are written on the PCB by the header pins, preceded with a '#' symbol) and then turn each of them on and off in turn. As the on-board stat LED is connected to I/O 1 I only needed to connect an LED and resistor to I/O 0 and 2 via the headers pins. That worked as expected but also using I/O 3 and 4 was a bit more difficult as they are used for USB communication and although the board's header pins connect directly to the microcontroller pins, both I/O 3 and 4 have series 22R resistors to USB D- and D+ respectively, and D- is also pulled up to VCC using a 1.5K resistor. However, I found that although I could use I/O 3, if I also used 4 it caused the power LED to blink off periodically and the sequence to pause as if the bootloader was running again (I checked that at this point the supply voltage drops low briefly, suggesting a reset). This happens if powering the board via USB, whether connected to a PC's USB port, or power adapter, but if powering the board via the header pins the sequence runs correctly and I can use I/O 0 to 4 without problems.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">It still remains the issue that using I/O 3 and 4 while the board is plugged into a PC can cause you program to behave oddly and the PC to report a bad USB device, so it's just as well the user program (sketch) runs after the bootloader when the board is plugged into USB, allowing us to program the board but it's best to not  have anything connected to I/O 3 and 4 (such as LEDs, for example), while the board is plugged into the PC. Instead, after uploading the sketch, disconnect the board, attach any components you need to, and then power it externally to check your program is running correctly.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section id="h.2f3abef249379c2_3" class="yaqOZd"><div class="IFuOkc"></div><div class="mYVXT"><div class="LS81yb class="C9DxTc " style="">D-FLIFE ATTINY88 Development Board</span></div></h3><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I bought the D-FLIFE ATTINY88 development board from Temu for just £1.60 ($2.07) and was described as a 'Digispark Compatible NANO V3.0' board and 'MH-ET LIVE Tiny88' with the following features:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">16.0Mhz microcontroller.</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Compatible with Arduino IDE 1.0+ (OSX/Win/Linux).</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Powered with 5V or 7-24V via USB or external power source (recommended 12V or lower, automatic selection).</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Equipped with a 500mA 5V voltage regulator on the board.</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Includes built-in USB.</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">26 I/O pins available (2 reserved for USB communication; all 26 can be used if USB communication is not active).</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">8k flash memory (approximately 6k available after program boot).</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Features on-board I2C and SPI interfaces.</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">There are 26 PWM pins available for software PWM, while hardware PWM is limited to only two pins (D9, D10). Additionally, there are 8 ADC pins, as well as Power LED and Test/Status LED.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I received with the board three headers; x1 3x2 male (for ISP) and x2 15-way male (GPIO). The board was very rough around the edges so could do with filing down.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">On the PCB top side we can be find:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">ISP and GPIO holes which you can solder headers to - labelled both sides except ISP.</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">x2 LEDs (green and red for power and user respectively)</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">78L05 5V regulator</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">RESET button</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">16MHz crystal</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Atmel T88-15MZ ATTINY88 12MHz 8-bit microcontroller 8KB flash</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Micro USB connector for power and programming</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br></span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">‘Tiny’ is written below the MCU (</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">microcontroller)</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">It seems different manufacturers make this board and there is no identification on the board I have who made it.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The datasheet for the MCU:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://www.mouser.co.uk/datasheet/2/268/doc8008-3445217.pdf" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://www.mouser.co.uk/datasheet/2/268/doc8008-3445217.pdf</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Although the MCU is rated for 12MHz maximum on the board they appear to be running it at 16MHz, due to the overclocking you may find issues with certain operations.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Note that because the MCU doesn't support USB the firmware is likely bit banging USB as do Digispark boards, for example.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Some information can be found here:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://github.com/SpenceKonde/ATTinyCore/issues/419" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://github.com/SpenceKonde/ATTinyCore/issues/419</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I plugged the board into my Windows 11 laptop, the green LED was on and the red LED rapidly flashed in bursts (possibly a preloaded test program). In the </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Windows </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Device Manager the board showed up as an Unknown device. To program the board I followed this guide using Arduino IDE:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://www.instructables.com/Getting-Started-With-MH-ET-LIVE-Tiny88-Arduino-Boa/" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://www.instructables.com/Getting-Started-With-MH-ET-LIVE-Tiny88-Arduino-Boa/</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I have had some experience with Micronucleus firmware when using the OLIMEXINO-85-KIT (which you can read about on my site further up this page).</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">During the install of the board the Installation Wizard reported it failed to install Digistump LLC (usbser) Ports, but it did install libusb-win32 Digispark Bootloader, libusb-win32 DigiUSB and Digistump LLC (digistump.com) (usbser) Ports.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I opened the Blink example as instructed, clicked the Upload button and when prompted to plug in the device I plugged the board into my laptop and it reported ‘Device is found!’ along with other messages, ending with 'Micronucleus done. Thank you!'. I could see from the messages that Micronucleus firmware v2.2 was used and despite Windows saying the USB device wasn't recognised, the upload was successful.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">After the upload, the red LED was flashing as expected of the Blink example. To further test I simply modified the Blink timing and uploaded again and noted that the blinking rate changed as expected. Note that if you want to keep the board plugged in, press the RESET button when prompted to plug in the device after clicking the upload button and it should upload successfully.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section id="h.7392025c2b6404db_7" class="yaqOZd"><div class="IFuOkc"></div><div class="mYVXT"><div class="LS81yb VICjCf j5pSsc db35Fc" tabindex="-1"><div class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd purZT-AhqUyc-II5mzb ZcASvf-AhqUyc-II5mzb pSzOP-AhqUyc-qWD73c Ktthjf-AhqUyc-qWD73c JNdkSc SQVYQc"><div class="JNdkSc-SmKAyb LkDMRd"><div class="" jscontroller="sGwD4d" jsaction="zXBUYb:zTPCnb;zQF9Uc:Qxe3nd;" jsname="F57UId"><div class="oKdM2c ZZyype Kzv0Me"><div id="h.7392025c2b6404db_4" class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd jXK9ad D2fZ2 zu5uec OjCsFc dmUFtb wHaque g5GTcb"><div class="jXK9ad-SmKAyb"><div class="tyJCtd mGzaTb Depvyb baZpAe"><div id="h.kmmnky3vt6uf" class="GV3q8e yMxPgf  aP9Z7e"></div><h3 id="h.kmmnky3vt6uf_l" dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q OmQG5e CDt4Ke " style=""><div jscontroller="Ae65rd" jsaction="touchstart:UrsOsc; click:KjsqPd; focusout:QZoaZ; mouseover:y0pDld; mouseout:dq0hvd;fv1Rjc:jbFSOd;CrfLRd:SzACGe;" class="CjVfdc"><div class="PPhIP rviiZ" jsname="haAclf"><div role="presentation" class="U26fgb mUbCce fKz7Od LRAOtb Znu9nd M9Bg4d" jscontroller="mxS5xe" jsaction="click:cOuCgd; Mega 2560 + WiFi) is an Arduino-like board which has the form factor of an Arduino Mega and is compatible with the Mega and Mega shields thanks to its AVR ATmega2560 MCU (with internal 256KB flash memory), although the WeMos Mega uses a USB micro instead of the full size USB socket of an original Arduino Mega. What makes the WeMos Mega different is that it also includes an Espressif ESP8266EX chip (with 4MB flash memory provided by 25Q32JVSIQ chip), adding 802.11 b/g/n 2.4GHz Wi-Fi functionality as well as additional I/O. While this makes for a very versatile board, essentially a dual micro system, providing network access without an add-on shield, it can prove complicated to use, as we will see later on. Note that there appears to be different manufacturers of the WeMos Mega (and as such some components and they way they are connected may differ), the particular Mega I have has no model identifier, just the WeMos and Wi-Fi logos.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Included on the board you get micro USB, reset button (located next to micro USB), antenna socket, power in jack (DC7-16V), mode push button switch (supposedly needs to be held down when programming the ESP but I didn't find that necessary). In addition to the standard Arduino Mega female connectors for interfacing and power, as we as the 3x2 male header for ICSP, there is also an additional 7x2 male header for </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">ESP GPIO</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""> (pinout on PCB underside) providing power and communication.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">An 8-way switch controls how the ESP/AVR communicate (8th setting has no use), and a 2-way switch selects RXDO/TXDO and RXD3/TXD3 (controls RXD/TXD; changes connecting port between ATmega2560 and ESP8266). Of the LEDs there are L (blue), ON (green), TX (blue), RX(blue), unlabelled (blue) LED controlled by ESP. There is a 16MHz crystal for the ATmega2560 and a 26MHz crystal for the ESP8266EX. </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Also of interest is a blank 16-pin chip, likely a CH340G as that's what the WeMos Mega shows up in Device manager as, and a MP2307DN step-down converter, which looks to be providing 5V for the board.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">On the PCB underside it has power ratings (I've reproduced as written):</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">DC In-7~16V</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">DC Out For 5V1.6A</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">DC Out for3.3V-1A</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I found a link to the schematic of a RobotDyn Mega WiFi R3, which appears to be very similar to the </span><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">WeMos Mega</span><span class="C9DxTc " style="">:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://3dprinting.stackexchange.com/questions/6316/arduino-wemos-and-ramps" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://3dprinting.stackexchange.com/questions/6316/arduino-wemos-and-ramps</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">It's worth studying the diagram to better understand how the two MCUs interact with each other.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Some observations regarding the schematic:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">'Power' is spelt wrong in two places.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">SW2 connects VCC either to 5V or 3.3V, on my WeMos version it has a TX/RX switch.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">There doesn't appear to be the 7x2 header.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The 2-way header controls power but is supposed to be the TX/RX switch as seen on actual board.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">As mentioned, while the board is a lot more versatile compared to a standard Arduino Mega, on the downside it can be more difficult to get working for those not familiar with the board. I always disconnect the board from my computer before changing the on-board switches, I'm not sure if that is absolutely necessary, however.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I will now go through the various modes, don't forget to set the port number in the Arduino IDE.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">On the PCB to the side of the 8-way switch it outlines the various modes, four of which are listed:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">MUC->ESP</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">USB->MCU</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">USB->ESP</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">GND-GPIO0</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">MUC/MCU represents ATMEGA2560, ESP is the ESP8266. Apart from GND-GPIO0, which is controlled solely with switch 7, the other four modes are  controlled by switch pairs. Example: MUC->ESP is enabled with both switch 1 and 2 on and the others off. Switch 7, when on, enables the programming mode of the ESP, when off the ESP program can be run (you may need to press the reset button) and serial access in the serial monitor.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The 2-way switch:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The switch is labelled in a somewhat confusing manner.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">RXD0 and TXD0 form USART0 of ATMEGA2560 and is always connected to D0/RX and D1/TX respectively. RXD3 and TXD3 form USART3 and is always connected to D15/RX3 and D14/TX3 respectively. What the switch is doing is setting whether the ESP8266 and ATMEGA2560 are connected via USART0 or USART3 in conjunction with the 8-way switch.</span><span class="C9DxTc " style=""><br><br></span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style="background-color: transparent; border-bottom: none; border-left: none; border-right: none; border-top: none; line-height: 1.656; margin-bottom: 0.0pt; margin-top: 0.0pt; padding-bottom: 0.0pt; padding-left: 0.0pt; padding-right: 0.0pt; padding-top: 0.0pt;"><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Now lets go through the various modes (note: 0=off, 1=on):</span></p><br><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style="background-color: transparent; border-bottom: none; class="jXK9ad-SmKAyb"><div class="tyJCtd mGzaTb Depvyb baZpAe"><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style=""> As this video is from early 2023 it suggests the kit was made available to buy at a similar time. This is the video I followed to assemble the kit and it took me just over 2 hours to finish, but as I highlight below there are a number of things to point out about the video, some of which slowed me down.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">No mention of anti-static precautions although a suitable looking mat has been used.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">At 7:54 no mention of snipping the switch pins which otherwise could pierce the battery when later fitted.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Even though the battery connector is the first thing to be soldered in the video, the connector is no longer attached to the PCB later in the video. It's not mentioned but it would have been better to solder the connector after the headers as it can get in the way when soldering them. </span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">At 22:16 suddenly the OLED header appears soldered to the PCB with no mention of soldering it even though it's required before soldering the display to it. Also, the video should have highlighted the need to snip the header pins on the OLED side.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">At 22:53 suddenly the Pro Micro board has been soldered to the headers. Because I had soldered the edge connector first (which they do at 21:11) it was tricky to solder the micro board as the connector was in the way.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">At 30:35 they go on to putting together the case but it would have been better to have done a first test of the electronics, although it doesn't take too long to remove the case should there be an electronic fault.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The screws that hold in the display, although not really necessary as it shouldn't be possible to press down on the top piece of plastic enough to do harm to the screen, are completely missed out from the video, explaining why I had two screws, spacers, and nuts left over. I couldn't see the display screws on any of the images on the 8BitCADE site (doesn't help they keep showing the same 3D render which omits them) but on an Amazon page, for example, I could just about see them. Since I worked out what the leftover pieces were for later rather than sooner it was tricky to fit the spacers between the display and the PCB and then fit the M2 screws, and even when I did get the screws in the nuts wouldn't stay on when put on the end of the screws, as if the screws were too short. Note that if you don't get the screws in flush with the display the top plastic piece won't go on, so perhaps it's best to not bother with them.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section id="h.604d6287d4322f76_3" class="yaqOZd"><div class="IFuOkc"></div><div class="mYVXT"><div class="LS81yb VICjCf j5pSsc db35Fc" tabindex="-1"><div class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd purZT-AhqUyc-II5mzb ZcASvf-AhqUyc-II5mzb pSzOP-AhqUyc-qWD73c Ktthjf-AhqUyc-qWD73c JNdkSc SQVYQc"><div class="JNdkSc-SmKAyb LkDMRd"><div class="" jscontroller="sGwD4d" jsaction="zXBUYb:zTPCnb;zQF9Uc:Qxe3nd;" jsname="F57UId"><div class="oKdM2c ZZyype Kzv0Me"><div id="h.604d6287d4322f76_0" class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd jXK9ad D2fZ2 zu5uec OjCsFc dmUFtb wHaque g5GTcb"><div class="jXK9ad-SmKAyb"><div class="tyJCtd mGzaTb Depvyb baZpAe"><div id="h.ttpg3xa201w0" class="GV3q8e yMxPgf  aP9Z7e"></div><h3 id="h.ttpg3xa201w0_l" dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q OmQG5e CDt4Ke " style=""><div jscontroller="Ae65rd" jsaction="touchstart:UrsOsc; Whereas the kit will set you back around £40 ($50) I was able to get it complete but lightly used from eBay for shy of £19.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">In the kit you get an Arduino Uno R3 compatible DFRduino UNO R3 microcontroller board, a number of sensors, lights, switches, wires, breadboard, and prototyping shield contained in a plastic box. Each component is packaged individually and clearly labelled, which is great for beginners to quickly locate components but not so good for the environment. As well as a Getting started card which includes links and lists of components in English and Chinese, also included are 15 project cards showing breadboard layout and the required components.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The product page can be found at:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="https://www.dfrobot.com/product-345.html" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">https://www.dfrobot.com/product-345.html</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Links on the site includes a link to a downloadable 'Arduino Getting Started tutorial' PDF, which introduces the Arduino platform, installing software, as well as details of the various projects that can be made with the kit, which includes explaining what the various components do and of the concepts of the microcontroller world such as I/O. Although well written, as to be expected of a Chinese product there are some less than perfect translations and some misleading text. For example, in one section it is explained that different types of variables take up different amounts of space and that the microcontroller in the Uno has 32K, which is incorrect as that 32K is for program storage, not variable storage which is stored in RAM. I also noticed mistakes in the code such as missing parentheses, semicolon, etc. which could easily cause the beginner to slip up. This brings to the other but related problem with the kit, as far as I can tell the Arduino project sketches aren't downloadable and have to be copied into the Arduino IDE text editor but that results in less that desirable formatting and comments spilling on to the next line, and multiple 'error: stray '\343' in program' and similar errors when trying to compile the sketch. Copying into Notepad and then into the IDE didn't help and copying sections at a time to the IDE wasn't a fix either although some parts copied didn't introduce errors. I ended up typing by hand into the IDE the code that wouldn't work when copied as some parts when copied didn't result in any errors.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section id="h.55e5b697a4be240d_41" class="yaqOZd"><div class="IFuOkc"></div><div class="mYVXT"><div class="LS81yb class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">82C54 Timer Test</span></div></h3><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">I needed a timer chip for a project I was working on (see </span><a class="XqQF9c" href="/site/jamesskingdom/Home/computers-exposed/create-your-own-computer/create-your-own-game-console" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="font-variant: normal; text-decoration: underline;">GameBird</span></a><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">) and found I had a number of 82C54 timer IC's which each contain 3 independent 16-bit down counters. The counters can each be set to 1 of 6 modes (with binary/BCD selection) and they have their own clock inputs (maximum of 8MHz for the standard version), counter outputs, and gate inputs (enabling/disable counting). Note that depending on the manufacturer there may be 2 letters before the part name, e.g. CS82C54.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">You can view the datasheet at:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="http://www.intersil.com/content/dam/Intersil/documents/82c5/82c54.pdf" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="font-variant: normal; text-decoration: underline;">http://www.intersil.com/content/dam/Intersil/documents/82c5/82c54.pdf</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="font-variant: normal;">Let's look at the circuit for the test:</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section id="h.55e5b697a4be240d_46" class="yaqOZd"><div class="IFuOkc"></div><div class="mYVXT"><div class="LS81yb VICjCf j5pSsc db35Fc" tabindex="-1"><div class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-zQtlcf Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-zQtlcf purZT-AhqUyc-II5mzb ZcASvf-AhqUyc-II5mzb pSzOP-AhqUyc-qWD73c Ktthjf-AhqUyc-qWD73c JNdkSc SQVYQc"><div class="JNdkSc-SmKAyb LkDMRd"><div class="" jscontroller="sGwD4d" jsaction="zXBUYb:zTPCnb;zQF9Uc:Qxe3nd;" jsname="F57UId"><div class="oKdM2c ZZyype Kzv0Me"><div id="h.55e5b697a4be240d_49" class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-zQtlcf Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-zQtlcf jXK9ad D2fZ2 zu5uec OjCsFc dmUFtb wHaque g5GTcb"><div class="jXK9ad-SmKAyb"><div class="tyJCtd baZpAe"><div class="t3iYD"><img src="https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/sitesv/AA5AbUB30y-f1eDlfT6Kwun9PgbCqChc3vc4jw9-KXFeISyMVGWXHOPXjzrO0Vj9IYbBUzFqQ6h1-rl2yxjhhNjLlXkVTUCKFo6-Iw-QsL6M0FSLh1d9zeiro-tiBFLRp1ZpiXneWqxsd65huYTSpPuvdjY0MIbY12mrWV7XI72Mi2YbFcnbzOlc5LXYKH1OgAMb4mShXdSg=w1280" class="CENy8b" role="img" style="width: 100%; margin: -0.0094873123% 0 -0.0094873123% 0%"></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div><div class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-R6PoUb Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-R6PoUb JNdkSc SQVYQc L6cTce-purZT L6cTce-pSzOP"><div class="JNdkSc-SmKAyb LkDMRd"><div class="" jscontroller="sGwD4d" jsaction="zXBUYb:zTPCnb;zQF9Uc:Qxe3nd;" jsname="F57UId"></div></div></div></div></div></section><section id="h.55e5b697a4be240d_53" class="yaqOZd"><div class="IFuOkc"></div><div class="mYVXT"><div class="LS81yb VICjCf j5pSsc db35Fc" tabindex="-1"><div class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd purZT-AhqUyc-II5mzb ZcASvf-AhqUyc-II5mzb pSzOP-AhqUyc-qWD73c Ktthjf-AhqUyc-qWD73c JNdkSc SQVYQc"><div class="JNdkSc-SmKAyb LkDMRd"><div class="" jscontroller="sGwD4d" jsaction="zXBUYb:zTPCnb;zQF9Uc:Qxe3nd;" jsname="F57UId"><div class="oKdM2c ZZyype Kzv0Me"><div id="h.55e5b697a4be240d_50" class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd jXK9ad D2fZ2 zu5uec OjCsFc dmUFtb wHaque g5GTcb"><div class="jXK9ad-SmKAyb"><div class="tyJCtd mGzaTb Depvyb baZpAe"><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">An Arduino Uno (or similar) communicates with the 82C54 via the data bus (D0 to D7), 2 address lines (A0 & A1), WR and RD; the 82C54 is always selected as CS is tied low. The 82C54 was designed with the 8086/8088 CPU in mind and that is why there are separate WR and RD inputs.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">A crystal oscillator generates a square wave of 4MHz which feeds into the three clock inputs of the 82C54 (CLK0-CLK2). The 3 gate inputs (GATE0-GATE2) are always held high so that the counters always run. To check that the timer is running correctly use an oscilloscope or logic analyzer to monitor the 3 outputs (OUT0-OUT2) separately or together.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The Arduino code for this test is available to download from the bottom of this page and is called 'Timer_82C54_Test.ino'. In the setup function you will find a number of test function calls, most of which have been commented out. They are as follows:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">test1()</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Test counter 0 in mode 3; only write MSB of initial count</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">test2()</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Test counter 0 in mode 3; write least significant byte first, then most significant byte</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">test3()</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Test counter 0 in mode 2; only write MSB of initial count</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">test4()</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Test all 3 counters in mode 3; only write MSB of initial count</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">To have a particular test run simply uncomment the test function and make sure the others are commented out, and then upload to the Arduino. The first test will have counter 0 output a square wave (mode 3) by specifying the most significant byte of the initial count value only. Test 2 does the same as test 1 but both the least and most significant bytes are specified. Also, there is extra code in setup() for test 2 which outputs to the serial monitor the hex 16-bit value of counter 0, 10 times. Depending on the value used for the counter and whether a different clock input to the timer is used you should see the values go lower each time. Note that if the counter timing is very short then it's possible that a value that follows will be higher than the previous. As for test 3 it puts counter 0 into mode 2, the rate generator mode, which outputs a brief pulse when the count goes to 1. Lastly, test 4 makes use of all 3 counters in square wave mode, giving the counters each their own counter value.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The program is a bit more complicated than perhaps it should be due to writing directly to the Arduino ports in setDataByte() and similar, the direct reading of the ports in readDataByte(), although the code could be simplified somewhat. The issue is that the first usable digital I/O pin of the Arduino is D2 as D0 and D1 are used for serial communication so we have to shift the data bits and split them over port D and port B. In addition, we have to combine other signals with port B. I did, however, take a shortcut with setting the data pins to input and output by using a loop (see setDataWrite() and setDataRead()). Note that there is a fair amount of code behind the various Arduino functions such as setDataWrite(), so they are quite slow. The delays I have put in using the delay() function could actually be shorter, in the microseconds.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">For the repetitive signal modes you can easily work out the frequency:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">output frequency (Hz) = input frequency (Hz) / count</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Where input frequency is the frequency of the signal fed into CLK0, CLK1, or CLK2, and count is the initial count. The maximum count is actually 0 not 0xFFFF, when in binary mode, as the down counter will happily start on 0 and then decrease to 0xFFFF.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">To calculate the pulse period:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">pulse period (s) = 1 / output frequency (Hz)</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">I tried two different crystal oscillators for this test and experimented with different timing values as I wanted to make sure that I could get the timer to work before I used it in my project.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section id="h.4f87f5c5c0ca5661_3" class="yaqOZd"><div class="IFuOkc"></div><div class="mYVXT"><div class="LS81yb VICjCf j5pSsc db35Fc" tabindex="-1"><div class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd purZT-AhqUyc-II5mzb ZcASvf-AhqUyc-II5mzb pSzOP-AhqUyc-qWD73c Ktthjf-AhqUyc-qWD73c JNdkSc SQVYQc"><div class="JNdkSc-SmKAyb LkDMRd"><div class="" jscontroller="sGwD4d" jsaction="zXBUYb:zTPCnb;zQF9Uc:Qxe3nd;" jsname="F57UId"><div class="oKdM2c ZZyype Kzv0Me"><div id="h.4f87f5c5c0ca5661_0" class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd jXK9ad D2fZ2 zu5uec OjCsFc dmUFtb wHaque g5GTcb"><div class="jXK9ad-SmKAyb"><div class="tyJCtd mGzaTb Depvyb baZpAe"><div id="h.fqs71uquai71" class="GV3q8e yMxPgf  aP9Z7e"></div><h3 id="h.fqs71uquai71_l" dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q OmQG5e CDt4Ke " style=""><div jscontroller="Ae65rd" jsaction="touchstart:UrsOsc; style="">The example sketch sets up two EEPROM objects, one located at address 0 - which is the physical one we have connected - and another at address 2 - which we don't have connected - and demonstrates that the code is actually working since it should return errors if there isn't actually an EEPROM at that address 2. So 'badEprom' didn't actually need changing unless you actually wanted to connect one at address 2.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style="background-color: transparent; border-bottom: none; border-left: none; border-right: none; border-top: none; line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 10.0pt; margin-top: 10.0pt; padding-bottom: 0.0pt; padding-left: 0.0pt; padding-right: 0.0pt; padding-top: 0.0pt;"><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Since up to eight AT24C chips can be connected you would need to create an object with the appropriate address and type for each one. Without specifying the correct type the sketch will report the wrong size (which is just a value passed to the main class) and I found when it prints out the long string some of the characters didn’t display correctly unless the correct constructor was used. This is possibly because of the different page size that gets passed to the constructor.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style="background-color: transparent; border-bottom: none; border-left: none; border-right: none; border-top: none; line-height: 1.38; margin-bottom: 10.0pt; margin-top: 10.0pt; padding-bottom: 0.0pt; padding-left: 0.0pt; padding-right: 0.0pt; padding-top: 0.0pt;"><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The chip appeared to be working correctly as the serial monitor displayed the expected values and indeed I tried a second AT24C64 and that also tested fine.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section id="h.55e5b697a4be240d_126" class="yaqOZd"><div class="IFuOkc"></div><div class="mYVXT"><div class="LS81yb VICjCf j5pSsc db35Fc" tabindex="-1"><div class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd purZT-AhqUyc-II5mzb ZcASvf-AhqUyc-II5mzb pSzOP-AhqUyc-qWD73c Ktthjf-AhqUyc-qWD73c JNdkSc SQVYQc"><div class="JNdkSc-SmKAyb LkDMRd"><div class="" jscontroller="sGwD4d" jsaction="zXBUYb:zTPCnb;zQF9Uc:Qxe3nd;" jsname="F57UId"><div class="oKdM2c ZZyype Kzv0Me"><div id="h.55e5b697a4be240d_123" class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd jXK9ad D2fZ2 zu5uec OjCsFc dmUFtb wHaque g5GTcb"><div class="jXK9ad-SmKAyb"><div class="tyJCtd mGzaTb Depvyb baZpAe"><div id="h.kaujlec324d7" class="GV3q8e yMxPgf  aP9Z7e"></div><h3 id="h.kaujlec324d7_l" dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q OmQG5e CDt4Ke " style=""><div jscontroller="Ae65rd" jsaction="touchstart:UrsOsc; click:KjsqPd; focusout:QZoaZ; mouseover:y0pDld; mouseout:dq0hvd;fv1Rjc:jbFSOd;CrfLRd:SzACGe;" class="CjVfdc"><div class="PPhIP rviiZ" jsname="haAclf"><div role="presentation" class="U26fgb mUbCce fKz7Od LRAOtb Znu9nd M9Bg4d" jscontroller="mxS5xe" jsaction="click:cOuCgd; mousedown:UX7yZ; mouseup:lbsD7e; mouseenter:tfO1Yc; mouseleave:JywGue; focus:AHmuwe; blur:O22p3e; contextmenu:mg9Pef;" jsshadow="" aria-describedby="h.kaujlec324d7_l" aria-label="Copy heading link" aria-disabled="false" data-tooltip="Copy heading link" aria-hidden="true" data-tooltip-position="top" data-tooltip-vertical-offset="12" data-tooltip-horizontal-offset="0"><a class="FKF6mc TpQm9d" href="#h.kaujlec324d7" aria-label="Copy heading link" jsname="hiK3ld" role="button" aria-describedby="h.kaujlec324d7_l"><div class="VTBa7b MbhUzd" jsname="ksKsZd"></div><span jsslot="" class="xjKiLb"><span class="Ce1Y1c" style="top: -11px"><svg class="OUGEr QdAdhf" width="22px" height="22px" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="currentColor" focusable="false"><path d="M0 0h24v24H0z" fill="none"></path><path d="M3.9 12c0-1.71 1.39-3.1 3.1-3.1h4V7H7c-2.76 0-5 2.24-5 5s2.24 5 5 5h4v-1.9H7c-1.71 0-3.1-1.39-3.1-3.1zM8 13h8v-2H8v2zm9-6h-4v1.9h4c1.71 0 3.1 1.39 3.1 3.1s-1.39 3.1-3.1 3.1h-4V17h4c2.76 0 5-2.24 5-5s-2.24-5-5-5z"></path></svg></span></span></a></div></div><span class="C9DxTc " style="">AT93C46 Test</span></div></h3><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">The AT93C46 is a 1Kb EEPROM chip that uses a '3 wire' interface and can be configured as either 128 x 8 or 64 x 16, making it suitable for storing settings or an ID for a system. It is simple to use and can be programmed a million times and it is claimed the data will be held for 100 years. </span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">You can find the datasheet here:</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><a class="XqQF9c" href="http://ee-classes.usc.edu/ee459/library/datasheets/AT93C46.pdf" target="_blank" style="color: inherit; text-decoration: none;"><span class="C9DxTc aw5Odc " style="text-decoration: underline;">http://ee-classes.usc.edu/ee459/library/datasheets/AT93C46.pdf</span></a></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">To test out the AT93C46 I wrote an Arduino program which you can find attached to the bottom of this page as 'AT93C46_EEPROM_Test.zip'. Download the file, un-zip it and upload the program to an Arduino Uno or similar.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Hardware connections to the AT93C46 can be found near the beginning of the file in the 'Hardware setup' section. The chip uses a serial interface involving DI for data input, DO for data output, and SK for the clock (maximum 2MHz). There is also the chip select (CS) input which is active high and permits the transfer of data. To read from the chip or write to it you need to send it an instruction which for reading requires a single instruction but for writing you have to enable programming first, do the write and then disable programming, so there are 3 instructions needed for writing.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">In the setup function we define our inputs and outputs and set the default state for the outputs. Next we set serial port data rate and turn on the built-in LED (labelled 'L' on the Arduino Uno) to show we are about to access the EEPROM. Once that is done we enter a loop and read in 16 bytes (addresses 0 to 15), output the current memory byte to the serial port, increase the value by 1, write the new value back and then display the new value by reading it again to make sure it was actually written. The built-in LED is then turned off to show that accessing the EEPROM  has stopped.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">If you have a programmer that supports the AT93C46, such as the MiniPro, you can use that to further check that the chip was written correctly. Something to be aware of is that the Arduino restarts whenever it is plugged into a computer or power source, after uploading a program to it, and when you enter or exit the serial monitor. That means if you do any of those things the EEPROM will get written with new values and that is one of the reasons why I made use of the built-in LED so it's clear when the chip is being updated.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">In the main loop of setup() we call the readByte() function to read a memory location from the EEPROM by supplying the address as the input parameter and receiving the byte read as the return value. Function readByte sets CS high, outputs the opcode (binary 10 for read), sends the address to read from, reads in a dummy bit and then the actual byte and lastly takes CS low.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">As for writeByte() it is a bit more difficult as we first enable writing by calling writeEnable() since the chip starts up with writing disabled. Then we call writeByteMain() with the address of the memory location to be updated and the value to be written there. The last thing to do is call writeDisable() to turn off writing. Since we are using a loop to update a number of memory locations we could have enabled programming once at the start of the loop and then disabled programming at the end of the loop.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Both writeEnable() and writeDisable() use 00 for the opcode but it is the address (more a control word than an address) that we send that signifies the type of programming instruction to use. Function writeByteMain() uses opcode 01 for write and the function is similar to readByte() but there is no dummy bit and we output a byte rather than receive one in. Note that in the main loop we wait 10ms using delay(10) to make sure programming has finished but you could probably use a shorter delay.</span></p><p dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q CDt4Ke " style=""><span class="C9DxTc " style="">Other instructions are supported by the AT93C46, such as to erase or write all memory with one value, so feel free to add them if you like.</span></p></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></div></section><section id="h.55e5b697a4be240d_102" class="yaqOZd"><div class="IFuOkc"></div><div class="mYVXT"><div class="LS81yb VICjCf j5pSsc db35Fc" tabindex="-1"><div class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd purZT-AhqUyc-II5mzb ZcASvf-AhqUyc-II5mzb pSzOP-AhqUyc-qWD73c Ktthjf-AhqUyc-qWD73c JNdkSc SQVYQc"><div class="JNdkSc-SmKAyb LkDMRd"><div class="" jscontroller="sGwD4d" jsaction="zXBUYb:zTPCnb;zQF9Uc:Qxe3nd;" jsname="F57UId"><div class="oKdM2c ZZyype Kzv0Me"><div id="h.55e5b697a4be240d_99" class="hJDwNd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd Ft7HRd-AhqUyc-uQSCkd jXK9ad D2fZ2 zu5uec OjCsFc dmUFtb wHaque g5GTcb"><div class="jXK9ad-SmKAyb"><div class="tyJCtd mGzaTb Depvyb baZpAe"><div id="h.xompw3dtxutc" class="GV3q8e yMxPgf  aP9Z7e"></div><h3 id="h.xompw3dtxutc_l" dir="ltr" class="zfr3Q OmQG5e CDt4Ke " style=""><div jscontroller="Ae65rd" jsaction="touchstart:UrsOsc;
